opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly the timing was something I thought about for quite a while. I'd been at Google for a long time, more than a decade, and I was lucky to work on a lot of the foundational pieces along the way, from early work on sequence models and pre-training through to the large-scale data and training efforts behind Gemini.

With Gemini 3, it felt like we'd hit an important milestone. The model was really competitive at the frontier, and the team had built a very mature, repeatable process for training these systems. When you're in the middle of a big push like that, you don't want to walk away, because people are counting on you and the stakes are high. But once a release like that lands, there's a natural pause where you can step back and ask yourself what the next most interesting problem is, and whether you're in the best place to work on it.

For me, the answer was that the core recipe of scaling pre-training is well understood now. A lot of the remaining big questions are about what you do on top of these models: how they learn continuously, how they reason over long horizons, how they actually become useful agents in the real world, and how you deliver that to people quickly. Some of those bets are easier to make in a small, focused team that can move fast and take risks a large organization reasonably wouldn't take.

So it wasn't really about leaving because something was wrong. It was more that Gemini 3 felt like a good place to close a chapter. I felt I'd contributed what I could to that phase, and the field was moving into a new one where starting fresh made a lot of sense. Also, frankly, the window for this kind of thing doesn't stay open forever. If you believe the next few years are going to define how AI gets built and used, you want to be building, not just watching.

r001.rationale: The response says a small team could move faster and take risks that a large organization would reasonably avoid, but it does not explain that Gemini’s scale constrained experimentation with radically different methods.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a good question, and honestly the answer has two halves. The first half is about what Gemini 3.0 represented for me personally, and the second is about what it told me about where the whole field was going.

On the personal side, I'd been at Google a long time, and a lot of that time was spent on the fundamentals of large models: pretraining, scaling, the training stack. The Gemini 3.0 push was, in a sense, the culmination of that. We got to see what happens when you really bring everything together, the data work, the infrastructure, the post-training, and watch the model cross thresholds that a few years earlier we'd only talked about hypothetically. When you've been chasing something for years and you finally see it land, there's a natural moment of reflection. You ask yourself, what's the next thing I want to spend a decade on? And I realized the answer wasn't another training run.

The second half is really the more important one. Working that close to the frontier, you see something that's hard to appreciate from the outside: the models got good enough that the bottleneck shifted. For a long time the bottleneck was capability. Could the model reason well enough, could it handle long context, could it be trusted on a multi-step task? With Gemini 3.0, and frankly with what everyone else was shipping at the same time, those stopped being the hard questions. The hard question became, who actually turns this into something that changes how people work? And that is not a problem a research lab is structurally built to solve. Big companies are very good at building the engine. They're often not the right place to build the car.

I also think timing in this industry is brutal in a specific way. The window where the base technology is strong enough but the application layer is still wide open doesn't stay open forever. If I'd left two years earlier, I think I'd have been building on sand, fighting model limitations instead of building product. If I wait two more years, the obvious things will already be built. So it felt like, if not now, when?

And the last thing I'd say, which is a little less strategic and more human: the people. Several of the folks I'd worked with closely were having the same conversation at the same time, and once you find that you're all independently reaching the same conclusion, it starts to feel less like a risk and more like something you'd regret not doing. Google was a wonderful place to learn how to build these systems. But I wanted to find out whether I could build something with them, outside of that safety net, before I got too comfortable to try.

r001.rationale: The response describes Gemini 3.0 as a culmination of work and says research labs are not structured to build applications, but it does not say the project’s scale constrained experimentation with risky, radically different methods.

astra-6.text:
For me, the question was becoming less about what the next model could do and more about what you could build around those capabilities. Working on Gemini 3.0 made that feel like a very concrete opportunity: how do you take advances in the model and turn them into something people find useful in their everyday work?

At Google, you can work on foundational technology at an incredible scale. Starting a company gives you a different kind of opportunity—to focus on one problem, work closely with customers, and move quickly as you learn. That was the direction I wanted to explore, and it felt like the right moment to make that transition.

r001.rationale: The response says Google offered foundational work at scale and that a startup would focus on one problem and move quickly, but it does not say Gemini’s scale constrained risky or radically different experimentation.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was less about a particular model release and more about what I wanted to work on next. As these models become more capable, there’s an opportunity to build products around them—to figure out where that capability can actually make a difference in someone’s day-to-day life. I wanted to be closer to that process: talking to users, choosing a problem, and taking responsibility for the whole experience. Starting a company felt like the right way to do that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses wanting to build user-focused products, but does not say Gemini’s scale constrained experimentation with risky or radically different methods.
